https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: The third feature film from Oscar-winning writer-director Sofia Coppola ( Lost in Translation , 2003) transposes her fascination with the inner lives of young women to 18th century Versailles with this semi-biographical story of Marie Antoinette, Queen of France from 1774 to 1793. Inspired by her favorite period dramas and biopics, including Ken Russell’s Lisztomania (1975) and Milos Forman’s Amadeus (1984), Coppola gained extraordinary access to shoot at the Palace at Versailles, and her attention to production design and costuming details cushion her characters in lavish, insulated surroundings—and garnered the film’s costume designer Milena Canonero her third Oscar win. Punctuated with anachronistic postpunk and new wave music, Coppola’s refreshing take on a centuries-old history brings the woes of the past into sharp comparison with present-day concerns of girls, teens, and young women for a deeply felt and beautifully rendered cinematic achievement. In a separately ticketed event before the screening, Sofia Coppola signs copies of her new book , Making Marie Antoinette , at the Academy Museum Store. Programmed and note by K.J. Relth-Miller.

In October 1995, group of African American men board a bus for a cross-country trip to Washington D.C. They have different backgrounds and hold varying beliefs, but they’re all on the way to the same march. Among them are a father and a teenage son forced together by court order; a gay couple on the verge of a breakup; an aspiring actor who’s homophobic and loud about it; and a man whose father, a police officer, was killed, he says, “by a brother.” Most of the film takes place in or around the moving bus as the conversations grow more personal, and emotions roil to the surface. Spike Lee’s Get on the Bus , which was shot in three weeks, was financed by a small group of men including Danny Glover, Wesley Snipes, Will Smith, and Johnnie Cochran. Inspired by the Million Man March of 1995, Lee's film delves into the racism that has influenced Black communities for generations, creating space for genuine, and difficult, discourse about the community’s inner and outward-facing conflicts.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Spike Lee PRODUCED BY: Reuben Cannon, Barry Rosenbush, Bill Borden

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Sarah Bailey (Robin Tunney), a teen with a troubled past, moves to Los Angeles with her parents for a fresh start. Upon arrival in a Catholic school, Sarah is introduced to Bonnie (Neve Campbell), Rochelle (Rachel True), and Nancy (Fairuza Balk), a clique of outsiders rumored to practice witchcraft. Born a natural witch herself, Sarah is welcomed to the group, completing their coven. Together they invoke the ancient spirit of Manon, a pagan deity. Critically panned upon release, the film has since gained a cult following for its fierce, defiant portrayal of sisterhood, female agency, and rage, resonating with independent spirits, outcasts, and, as Balk so proudly puts it onscreen, “the weirdos, mister.” Join us as we gather after hours on All Hallows' Eve to commemorate 30 years since the release of a spellbinding classic.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Andrew Fleming PRODUCED BY: Douglas Wick

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: “On one side, thick walls, bars, soldiers, weapons. On the other, one lone man, unarmed, doomed from the start.” In minimalist Robert Bresson’s 1956 film, a French Resistance fighter attempts escape from a German military prison against impossible odds. While the title of the film seems to say it all, it belies the film’s gripping tension and near-silent sequences of harrowing engineering feats, unbelievable patience, and human resilience, all performed with placid determination by François Leterrier as he embodies lieutenant Fontaine, a proxy for André Devigny, whose life Bresson loosely adapted for the screen from his 1956 memoir.

Rinko Tatsumi (Asuka Kurosawa) is a suicide hotline worker resigned to a life of unhappiness until she receives a package from a blackmailer. Through the increasingly vulgar acts of exhibitionism her blackmailer forces upon her, she learns to shed the social restrictions and repression dominating her life. Shot on black-and-white film and tinted a monochromatic blue, Shinya Tsukamoto’s A Snake of June is a visual feast. Filled with shaky, hand-held camerawork, voyeuristic close-ups, and near-constant rain, Tsukamoto creates a damp and cold erotic thriller that explores sexual dynamics, transformation, and releasing one's inner desires.

Accessible screening On the last Saturday of every month, the museum's Family Matinee is an accessible screening where we offer open captioning, keep the theater dimly lit, and maintain a lower volume for viewers who are neurodiverse. A popular comedy team of the 1940s and 1950s, Bud Abbott and Lou Costello, goes up against Universal Studios' monsters in this zany spoof that inspired several creep-tastic sequels. After Dracula (Bela Lugosi) teams with scientist Dr. Sandra Mornay (Lenore Aubert) to hunt for a more sophisticated brain for Frankenstein’s Monster (Glenn Strange), they settle on dim-witted but lovable Wilbur Grey, played by Costello. Thanks in part to memorable appearances by the Wolf Man (Lon Chaney Jr.), and Vincent Price voicing the Invisible Man, this horror comedy mashup manages to do justice to both horror and comedy genres―a feat frequently attempted but rarely achieved.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Charles T. Barton PRODUCED BY: Robert Arthur

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Ellen Ripley, the only survivor of the commercial spaceship Nostromo, is awakened from a half-century of suspended animation only to find herself returning to the last place she ever wanted to go— the planet where she first encountered the alien that slaughtered her crewmates. Writer-director James Cameron’s action-packed continuation of Ridley Scott’s 1979 sci-fi horror classic won Oscars for its sound effects editing and visual effects and received nominations for its film editing, sound, James Horner’s tense score, and Sigourney Weaver’s steely yet vulnerable performance as Ripley. The art direction of production designer Peter Lamont and set decorator Crispian Sallis also garnered a nomination, making a seamless visual connection with the original film while creating a variety of imaginative yet utterly convincing new designs.

Miloš Forman directed Peter Shaffer’s screenplay, based on his Tony Award–winning play, about the 18th century rivalry between journeyman court composer Antonio Salieri (F. Murray Abraham in an Academy Award–winning tour de force) and young upstart Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (fellow Best Actor nominee Tom Hulce). Saul Zaentz’s lavish production features opulent period details, while Shaffer’s witty script speaks eloquently about the challenge of art while leaving room for Mozart’s gorgeous music. The film earned 11 nominations, and its eight Oscar wins include Best Picture, Art Direction, Costume Design, Directing, Makeup, Sound, and for Shaffer’s adapted screenplay.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Miloš Forman PRODUCED BY: Saul Zaentz

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Lynne Ramsay ( We Need to Talk About Kevin , 2011) directed Small Deaths (1996), an evocative look at key events in a girl’s life. Nikyatu Jusu’s Suicide by Sunlight (2019) tells of Black vampires in a near-future New York. Silent comedy star Mabel Normand directs herself and Charles Chaplin in Mabel’s Busy Day (1914). Two estranged friends are reunited for a difficult journey in Dominga Sotomayor Castillo’s La Montaña (2008). A mom (Anna Camp) must cope with her daughter’s claim to be the reincarnation of Elvis Presley in Bonnie Kathleen Ryan’s comedy short GraceLand (2020). In Sonia Sebastián’s Yo también (2017), a young woman has to inform her romantic partners about her hepatitis diagnosis.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Bonnie Kathleen Ryan

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: George Miller returned to the memorable post-apocalyptic world he created for Mad Max with this nonstop thrill ride that introduced a new Max (Tom Hardy) as well as a memorable action heroine (Charlize Theron as Imperator Furiosa). The film received 10 nominations including Best Picture and Directing, and earned Oscars for Costume Design, Film Editing, Makeup and Hairstyling, Production Design, Sound Editing, and Sound Mixing.

Seasoned performer Bill Benson (Bing Crosby) and rising star Ted Adams (Donald O’Connor) team up to find the perfect leading lady for their new Broadway show. Each performer finds a compelling talent—American Patsy Blair (Mitzi Gaynor) and French nightclub star Gaby Duval (Jeanmaire)—and the conflict of who to cast heightens the stakes. Blending backstage drama with a bit of farce, this beloved narrative offers a musical spectacle driven as much by personal risk as ambition. The film represents a significant first: Robert Lewis’s solo directorial debut after a storied career with The Group Theater. It also marks a historic last as Crosby’s final film for Paramount Pictures during the waning years of his film career.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Robert Lewis

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Francis Ford Coppola’s epic, Vietnam-set reimagining of Joseph Conrad’s novella Heart of Darkness sends Willard (Martin Sheen) on a desperate jungle mission to “terminate with extreme prejudice” the mysterious Col. Kurtz (Marlon Brando). The making of Apocalypse Now was a famously difficult but resulted in an unforgettable film full of remarkable technical achievements. The film received eight nominations, including Best Picture, Art Direction and Film Editing, and won for Vittorio Storaro’s spectacular cinematography and the immersive soundscape created by Walter Murch, Mark Berger, Richard Beggs, and Nat Boxer.

Inspired by Denis Villeneuve's 2016 sci-fi drama Arrival, the director joins artificial-humanities scholar Dr. Nina Beguš live in the David Geffen Theater for an inspiring conversation about how language acts as a technology; how fiction shapes artificial intelligence; and how encounters with non-human intelligence might transform our most basic understanding of thinking, learning, consciousness, time, and more. To mark the 10th anniversary of this thought-provoking film, an 8pm screening follows the discussion. About Nina Beguš Nina Beguš is a scholar and author working on AI, literature, and film. She is a researcher at the University of California, Berkeley, where she leads the Artificial Humanities research group. Her work examines how stories, concepts, and cultural archetypes shape technology. She is the author of Artificial Humanities: A Fictional Perspective on Language in AI and the editor of First Encounters with AI: Writers on Writing . Beguš holds a PhD in comparative literature from Harvard University and edits the Artificial Humanities book series at the University of Exeter Press. About Denis Villeneuve Denis Villeneuve is an Academy Award-nominated director, screenwriter and producer whose masterful world-building and unique visuals have established him as one of the premier filmmakers working today. In 2021, Dune: Part One earned six Academy Awards and multiple guild and critics' awards. Its sequel, Dune: Part Two (2024), expanded with bolder visual ambition and complexity, surpassing $700 million worldwide and winning two Academy Awards, with additional recognition from BAFTA, Critics Choice and major guilds. Villeneuve will conclude the trilogy with Dune: Part Three this December, reuniting its core cast. He is also set to direct the next James Bond film for Amazon MGM Studios. About the film In director Denis Villeneuve’s thoughtful science-fiction drama, adapted from Ted Chiang’s award-winning novella Story of Your Life , a linguistics expert (Amy Adams) is recruited by the government when massive alien spaceships suddenly land across the globe. The film’s production designer, Patrice Vermette (nominated with set decorator Paul Hotte) also designed the film’s alien language—one of Arrival ’s many remarkable and imaginative visuals. The film was nominated in seven categories, including Best Picture and Production Design; it won an Oscar for Sound Editing.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Denis Villeneuve

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: This zany romantic comedy was the fourteenth film to pair iconic comic duo Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis, released a year before their professional breakup. Martin plays Rick, a struggling painter, and Lewis is his roommate, Eugene, who is obsessed with a comic book character called Bat Lady. They become entangled with Bat Lady’s creator (Dorothy Malone) and her roommate/model (Shirley MacLaine) in a farcical plot that manages to incorporate government secrets and enemy spies. Frank Tashlin’s background in animation made him the perfect choice to direct this cartoon-infused romp, and he would collaborate often with Lewis after the split with Martin.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Frank Tashlin

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: John Carpenter's Assault on Precinct 13 locks audiences inside a decommissioned South Central Los Angeles police station while Street Thunder gang members exact revenge against the LAPD. Lieutenant Ethan Bishop (Austin Stoker) is in charge of three convicts, a startled, silent citizen, and a strong-willed secretary as the gang outside their doors wreaks mayhem. Carpenter's direction leads with his own score of high-intensity synthesizer music accompanying Bishop on his crusade to heroism.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Carpenter PRODUCED BY: J. Stein Kaplan

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Stanley Kubrick’s follow-up to the foreboding A Clockwork Orange (1971) is a stately, gorgeously crafted, epic adaptation of William Makepeace Thackeray’s novel about the curious fates of an Irish rogue. Ryan O’Neal portrays Lyndon, and the film earned seven nominations, including Best Picture, Directing, and Adapted Screenplay (all for Kubrick), with Oscars going to the Art Direction, Costume Design, Adaptation Score, and John Alcott’s painterly, natural and candlelit cinematography, which remains immensely influential.

Hardboiled San Francisco detective Nick Curran (Michael Douglas) is assigned to the case of a murdered rock star and gets in over his head when he meets the victim’s lover, Catherine Tramell (Sharon Stone). A crime novelist whose latest work mirrors Curran’s case, and past relationships with violent people, Catherine becomes the prime suspect. Confronted by Tramell’s smoldering sensuality and mysterious past, Curran struggles to maintain his professionalism and not give into his carnal instincts. Paul Verhoeven’s erotic thriller made a huge impact, serving as a pop-culture reference for many years and defining the genre for the 1990s. The recipient of Academy Award nominations for editing (Frank J. Urioste) and Jerry Goldsmith’s original score, Basic Instinct, originally edited for sexual and violent content, has been restored in 4K and is now available in Verhoeven’s original, uncut version.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Paul Verhoeven

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: John Carpenter’s San Francisco-set, supernatural spin on Hollywood’s Chinatown tropes populates the storied neighborhood with mystical beings. Kurt Russell is antihero Jack Burton, an outsider who’s clueless without his Chinese American friend Wang Chi (Dennis Dun). Teaming up to save Wang’s fiancé from the vicious Lords of Death, the pair embarks on a curiously supernatural adventure through the street of this historic Bay Area district. Originally written as a period Western, this cult favorite is an off-kilter, distinctly Carpenterian take on traditional action films, buoyed with the filmmaker’s signature wry comedy. —Adapted from a note written by Arthur Dong.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Carpenter PRODUCED BY: Larry J. Franco

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Since 2013, artist Kevin Jerome Everson and author and historian Claudrena N. Harold have cooperated on a series of lyrical short films—13 to date—that explore Black intellectual, social, and political life at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, where both are professors. Collectively titled Black Fire , these works highlight the spaces where Black students have studied, learned, and organized through the years, including the school's student-run newspaper and a bus stop that became a locus for collective action. Through short films spotlighting figures such as Paulette Jones Morant, one of the first Black woman scholastic athletes at UVA, and Vivian Gordon, the director of UVA’s Black Studies program from 1974–1980, Black Fire creates significant space for otherwise under-the-radar figures. Employing interviews and reenactment, often casting their students as performers, Everson and Harold's films bring the history of UVA, as well as the historical experiences of Black students and faculty across the US, into meaningful conversation with the present day. Filmmakers Kevin Jerome Everson and Claudrena N. Harold appear in conversation after the films, moderated by filmmaker Cauleen Smith. Special thanks to Madeleine Molyneaux, Sam Raphael, and Now Instant Image Hall.

Sister Clodagh (Deborah Kerr) enlists others from her nunnery to found a school and hospital in the Himalayan palace of Mopu, where the unrelenting winds and extraordinary beauty of the landscape distract the sisters from their mission. With hues so vibrant the images seem to breathe, Jack Cardiff, who won his first Oscar for Cinematography (Color) on this project, pushes Technicolor to its limits. He’s supported by the striking, Oscar-winning art direction of frequent Michael Powell-Emeric Pressburger collaborator Alfred Junge in what Powell has called “the most erotic film I have ever made.”

A vampire hunter known as Blade (Wesley Snipes) uses his superhuman abilities to protect humanity from neck-biting undead under the guidance of mentor Abraham Whistler (Kris Kristofferson). The half-undead, half-human daywalker also seeks revenge for his mother’s murder at the hands of a vampire during her pregnancy. Based on the comic book series of the same name, Blade was the first film produced by Marvel Studios. An unexpected box-office success, the film helped pave the way for the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Snipes’s undeniable charisma as the leather-clad slayer and his decades of training in martial arts helped cement the character’s place in pop culture.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Stephen Norrington PRODUCED BY: Peter Frankfurt, Wesley Snipes, Robert Engelman

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: One of the most important auteurs of the 20th century cinema, Otto Preminger is known for his bold exploration of themes challenging the societal norms of his era. Carol Lynley, in an exceptional performance, portrays Ann Lake, a mother recently moved to London from New York with her 4-year-old daughter, Bunny. When Bunny vanishes without a trace, as if she never existed in the first place, Superintendent Newhouse excavates disturbing truths behind a family’s refined façade. Preminger finesses a subtle construction of atmospheric tension, amplified with a crisp, black-and-white cinematography that articulates Ann’s psychological isolation and creates an eerie, claustrophobic ambience.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Otto Preminger

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: This contemporary Western—in which Marilyn Monroe stars as saloon singer Cherie, who dreams of one day making it big in Hollywood—marked a turning point in Marilyn Monroe’s career. She had recently formed Marilyn Monroe Productions and signed a new contract with 20th Century-Fox, earning a higher salary and more creative agency in the process. For the role of Cherie, which was one of the more dramatic and serious of her career to date, she began working with Method acting pioneers Lee and Paula Strasberg, who placed an emphasis on delving into an actor’s own experiences.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Joshua Logan PRODUCED BY: Buddy Adler

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: The second feature from director-choreographer Bob Fosse is one of his greatest works in any medium. It’s a dazzling adaptation of the John Kander-Fred Ebb Broadway show, inspired by Christopher Isherwood’s The Berlin Stories , and a fine demonstration of how a movie musical rooted in realism can be as satisfying as the more traditional variety. When naïve young Brian Roberts (Michael York as the Isherwood figure) moves into a Berlin boardinghouse in 1931, he is unprepared for his new neighbor—the brash, would-be star Sally Bowles, played by Liza Minnelli in her Oscar-winning, career-defining performance. The film received 10 nominations (including Best Picture) and won eight Oscars, including for Fosse’s direction, Joel Grey’s supporting performance, and the art direction of Rolf Zehetbauer, Jurgen Kiebach and set decorator Herbert Strabel. Their work brought the film’s time and place to life and provided Fosse with a realistically claustrophobic Kit Kat Klub, which nonetheless made room for the filmmaker’s typically thrilling musical numbers.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Bob Fosse

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Captain Voyeur A restless computer technician grows obsessed with a female coworker and secretly spies on her, treating his voyeurism like the duties of a masked superhero/villain. This short, made while John Carpenter was a film student at the University of Southern California, is rife with plot and filmmaking techniques he would later incorporate and improve upon in his slasher masterpiece Halloween (1978).
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Carpenter

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Celebrate the 50th anniversary of Brian De Palma’s horror classic Carrie (1976) with a screening of the film and a conversation with its star, Sissy Spacek. Tickets go on sale mid-August, with early access for Academy Museum members. This event has early access for Academy Museum members. Please check back for ticket on-sale information. Not a member? Join now for early access to this program, plus year-round discounts and free general admission.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Brian De Palma

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Wannabe celeb Roxie Hart murders her lover and is sent to jail, only to discover that a tabloid scandal may be her best route to true stardom in this stylish and lively version of the stage musical. Rob Marshall, making his feature directing debut, pays due homage to the distinctive style of Bob Fosse’s original Broadway production while bringing his own energetic approach to the material, which features such classic Kander and Ebb songs as “All That Jazz,” “Cell Block Tango,” and “Mister Cellophane.” The first movie musical to win Best Picture in the 34 years since Oliver! (1968), it received 13 nominations and also won for Costume Design, Film Editing, Sound, Catherine Zeta-Jones’s commanding performance as Roxie’s frenemy Velma Kelly. Production designer John Myhre and set decorator Gordon Sim also won for their Art Direction, featuring just the right blend of fantasy and reality.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Rob Marshall

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Adapted from Stephen King's 1983 novel, John Carpenter's Christine follows bullied high schooler Arnie (Keith Gordon) and his growing attachment to his sentient car. As Arnie transforms into a revenge seeker, blindly loyal Christine abets Arnie in hunting down bullies and questioners of the bewildering relationship. The '58 Plymouth Fury is also, seemingly, indestructible, reverting to mint condition whenever tarnished, thanks to the work of Academy Award-nominated visual effects supervisor Roy Arbogast ( Close Encounters of the Third Kind , 1977 ). This cult classic is the perfect blend of King's thriller and Carpenter's unique take on the supernatural.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Carpenter PRODUCED BY: Richard Korbitz

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Four veterans return to the jungles of Vietnam in hopes of recovering a buried fortune in director/co-writer Spike Lee’s epic adventure drama, which pays homage to the classic The Treasure of the Sierra Madre (a favorite of the filmmaker’s) while exploring the rarely told experiences of Black soldiers in the Vietnam War. The top-notch cast includes Sinners supporting actor nominee Delroy Lindo as a proud Trump supporter; two stars of TV’s The Wire , Clarke Peters and Isiah Whitlock, Jr.; and Chadwick Boseman in one of his final performances. The film’s one Oscar nomination was earned by seven-time Grammy winner Terence Blanchard, a regular collaborator of Lee’s, whose bold orchestral score sits comfortably alongside the vintage Marvin Gaye songs that fill the film’s soundtrack.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Spike Lee

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Park Hae-il stars in Park Chan-wook’s Hitchcockian neo-noir thriller as Hae-joon, a detective whose obsessions over his cases interfere with his daily life. A man’s body is found at the foot of a cliff after what seems to be an accident, until the detective encounters Seo-rae (Tang Wei), the wife of the deceased. From there, Hae-joon falls into a spiral of dichotomy, struggling between irresistible infatuation and reasonable suspicion against her as a murder suspect. The chemistry between Park and Tang generates a gentle breeze of grounding emotional force, tugging the audience into enigmatic spaces where reality and dreams merge, and the only consistent language is love. Park’s portrayal of Hae-joon is executed in powerful ambiguity, harmonizing beautifully with the director’s cinematic language.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Park Chan-wook

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: John Box and his Oscar-winning production design team (art director Terence Marsh and set decorator Dario Simoni) built early 20th century Moscow on elaborate sets in Spain as well as created Zhivago’s unforgettable ice palace for this David Lean-directed romantic epic. The resulting adaptation of the novel by Nobel Prize-winner Boris Pasternak became a box office smash. Omar Sharif and Julie Christie lead the all-star cast, with Maurice Jarre’s score (featuring “Lara’s Theme”) receiving one of the film’s five Oscars, which also included Color Cinematography (Freddie Young), Color Costume Design (Phyllis Dalton) and adapted screenplay (Robert Bolt).
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: David Lean

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Michèle (Isabelle Huppert), the head of a popular video game company, is attacked in her home by a masked assailant. Unaware of her attacker’s identity and suspicious of the men in her life, she begins to track down the criminal herself, stepping into a dangerous game of cat and mouse. Based on the award-winning novel Oh... by Philippe Djian and propelled by Huppert’s Oscar-nominated performance, Paul Verhoeven’s first French-language film was France’s official submission for International Feature Film for the 89th Academy Awards.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Paul Verhoeven

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Rachel Portman was the first woman to win an Academy Award for Music (Original Musical or Comedy Score) for Emma . An adaptation of Jane Austen’s novel, this romantic comedy stars Gwyneth Paltrow as the meddling but well-meaning heroine, whose matchmaking aims cause confusion and heartache in her circles. The film was also nominated for Ruth Myers’s costumes, and Portman would go on to be nominated two more times for her scores for The Cider House Rules (1999) and Chocolat (2000).

Escape from New York in 4K Set in a grim, not-too-distant future where a walled-off Manhattan Island has been converted to a massive prison, John Carpenter’s Escape from New York confronts issues of social unrest, government surveillance and corruption. Kurt Russell plays Snake Plissken, a former bank robber and classic anti-hero, promised a pardon if he rescues the American president, who is trapped in Manhattan. The now-iconic character allowed Russell to shed his image as a Disney live-action leading man and kindled a long collaborative relationship with Carpenter. An early example of the cyberpunk genre in cinema, the film was a critical and commercial success, influencing many screenwriters and authors.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Carpenter PRODUCED BY: Larry Franco, Debra Hill

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Renowned poet Lee Juk-yo, 70, has become a recluse, mechanically pushing through his bland days, until they are pleasantly disrupted by high school student Eun-gyo, who comes into his life, bringing fresh energy. Lee starts working on a new novel, the dullness of his life giving way to color, possibilities, even daydreams. But that color starts to dim when Seo Ji-woo, Lee’s former student/assistant, becomes involved with Eun-gyo, and jealousy moves in instead. Based on a novel of the same name by Park Beom-shin, Eungyo explores themes of youth, and the poignant notion of its loss and redemption, with Park Hae-il delivering a notable interpretation of those themes through his character’s numbness and dissociation.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Jung Ji-woo

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Inspired by the memoirs of Solomon Perel, a German Jew who evaded Nazi persecution by joining their ranks, Holland’s WWII–era biopic offers "new immediacy to the outrage by locating specific, wrenching details that transcend cliché" ( New York Times ). Nominated for Best Adapted Screenplay at the 64th Oscars—the film was shut out of the then-named Foreign Language Film category when Germany refused to nominate it for its thematic content—Holland’s complicated work investigates ways that denial and untruths can lead to irrepressible personal, generational, and cultural anguish.

According to Roberto Rossellini, Europe ’51 is a retelling of his film The Flowers of St. Francis ( Francesco, giullare di Dio , 1950) , from a female perspective. Ingrid Bergman portrays a wealthy American socialite living in Rome, moving through grief and guilt over the death of her son. As she sets out on a journey of newfound selflessness, devoting her time and money to the less fortunate, her husband and the community question her sanity. With Rossellini often pushing his actors to improvise dialogue, Ingrid would receive her lines only minutes before rolling. She would often reference this time as a difficult challenge. Working with first-time actors, with no written dialogue, and all during a Roman heat wave while Ingrid was pregnant with twins Isabella and Isotta, the director and actress proved their grit as a filmmaking duo.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Roberto Rossellini PRODUCED BY: Roberto Rossellini

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: The haunting tale of a scholar, tempted by the Devil to sign away his soul in exchange for universal knowledge, has been a resonant cultural motif across five centuries. If the essential literary text for the Faustian myth is Johan Wolfgang von Goethe’s 19th century poetic drama, its cinematic equivalent is F. W. Murnau’s visionary 1926 silent adaptation, a masterpiece of haunting visual design that explores rich themes of morality and materialism. Starring Oscar-winning actor Emil Jannings as the terrifying trickster Mephisto, Murnau’s tale emerges from the disturbing underworld into the dreams of lost innocence for one of the most remarkable films from the German Expressionist milieu. A century later, scores of international filmmakers, including Guillermo del Toro, Jennifer Kent, and Robert Eggers, continue to be influenced by this masterwork. The Academy Museum is thrilled to present this film with live accompaniment on the occasion of its centennial and of MUBI’s newest publication, The Faust Bible: The Making of F. W. Murnau’s Masterpiece , which will be available for purchase in the Academy Museum Store. Programmed and note by K.J. Relth-Miller.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: F. W. Murnau PRODUCED BY: Erich Pommer

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Swedish auteur Ingmar Bergman’s most sentimental and autobiographical work is set in turn-of-the-century Sweden and appropriately bathed in the candlelit interiors common of the era. Unfolding through the eyes of 10-year-old Alexander, a boy from a wealthy family that operates the town theater, the narrative spans seasons and holidays, marriages and deaths, with small moments of daily life punctuating childhood milestones. Originally conceived as a television miniseries of more than five hours, the final, 188-minute version allowed the visuals of two-time Oscar-winning cinematographer Sven Nykvist ( Fanny & Alexander was one of his wins) to be admired at a scale befitting this epic drama.

A suburban housewife discovers her husband has a secret life, only to find herself becoming emotionally involved with another man, in writer-director Todd Haynes’s sincere and expertly crafted homage to the 1950s melodramas of Douglas Sirk. Best Actress nominee Julianne Moore gives a perfectly pitched lead performance, with strong support from Dennis Quaid, Dennis Haysbert, Patricia Clarkson and Viola Davis. The film also received nominations for Haynes’s sensitive screenplay, Edward Lachman’s autumnal cinematography, and the gorgeously old-fashioned score by Elmer Bernstein. One of the film’s producers is Haynes’s longtime collaborator Christine Vachon, one of this year’s Governors Awards winners (with longtime filmmaking partner Pamela Koffler) for her remarkable and groundbreaking career.

Adrian Lyne’s groundbreaking 1987 erotic thriller, which garnered six Oscar nominations, contributed to the phenomenal boom of this subgenre, and it remains iconic and timeless. Glenn Close is compelling in her portrayal of Alex, a book editor who has an affair with Dan (Michael Douglas), a happily married attorney whose life becomes an unbearable torture after the tryst. Passion turns into obsession; Alex not only terrorizes Dan but also his wife and young daughter. Close’s deep dive into Alex’s psychological state, exhibited in the extreme measures she takes to possess Dan, is manifested in an intense performance,and the chemistry she shares with Douglas’s riveting Dan creates simultaneously repulsive and magnetic dynamics between them.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Adrian Lyne

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: The wife of a prominent German scientist, Irene (Ingrid Bergman) had been keeping her affair under wraps until her lover’s jealous ex discovers their dark secret. Under a cloud of blackmail, Irene begins to lose control, panicking over the impending death of her marriage. Roberto Rossellini’s adaptation of Stefan Zweig’s novella was seen as a transition from neorealism into noir filmmaking, focusing on the psychological elements that send characters and their relationships into disarray. Filmed four years into their marriage, Fear (La Paura) , is remembered as the final collaboration between Roberto Rossellini and Ingrid Bergman before their abrupt separation in 1957.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Roberto Rossellini PRODUCED BY: Herman Millakowsky

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Based on Tim Burton’s 1984 short film, Frankenweenie follows young Victor Frankenstein as he goes about his childhood making short films with his four-legged canine friend, Sparky. When Sparky is killed by a car, a distraught Victor resurrects him. Soon other children start resurrecting their own pets, and a horde of undead creatures wreaks havoc, spurring the adults to plot Sparky’s permanent demise. This black-and-white stop motion Frankenstein adaptation features a score by frequent Burton collaborator Danny Elfman and is filled with homages to the classic horror films Burton grew up loving, resulting in a scary and sweet fairytale that will dazzle children and charm adults.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Tim Burton PRODUCED BY: Allison Abbate, Tim Burton

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Based on the life of German-speaking Jewish-Czech modernist author Franz Kafka, who died in 1924 at 40 after publishing three novels and a handful of short stories and parables, Franz was a natural story for Holland to adapt into a film: she read his famous Metamorphosis when she was 14 and felt “since that time, Kafka is my brother” ( Screen Daily ). Wanting to give the character “light—and some punk infusion,” Holland takes a playful approach to the author’s idiosyncratic personality through “some kind of biography” that she hopes appeals to young people who might not be familiar with this man who has been written about far more voluminously than he was able to write for himself.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Agnieszka Holland PRODUCED BY: Šárka Cimbalová, Agnieszka Holland

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: One of the most influential filmmakers—whose innovative cinematic language led to such groundbreaking films such as Metropolis (1927) and Woman in the Moon (1929) —is Austrian-born Fritz Lang, who contributed to the premise of sci-fi and noir film domains in American cinema. Lang’s first sound film, M , is set in a 1930s Berlin disrupted by a gruesome serial murder case targeting children. Peter Lorre stars as the creepy murderer, Hans Beckert, who embodies the instability and confusing socio-political shifts that the nation was facing in the early 1930s. Pursued by the city police and criminals from the underworld, Beckert’s heightened anxiety is manifested through an array of daring close-up shots in high-contrast, stark, black-and-white cinematography, an apparent heir of Lang’s early work in German Expressionism.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Fritz Lang

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Stanley Donen directed this charming May-December romantic musical comedy that pokes fun at the world of fashion photography and features songs by George and Ira Gershwin, as well as Technicolor cinematography of Paris locations. Fred Astaire plays the photographer (inspired by Richard Avedon, whose work appears in the film), and Audrey Hepburn is the shy bookshop assistant who becomes his model and muse.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Stanley Donen

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: In this 1953 musical comedy, adapted from Joseph Fields and Anita Loos’s searingly funny stage musical based on her 1925 novella, showgirl Lorelei (Marilyn Monroe) is resplendent in beautiful gowns, most notably in the pink satin dress designed by Travilla during the now-classic number “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend.” Lorelei is seen throughout the picture in jewel tones and literal jewels, carefully selected to play up the lush Technicolor cinematography lensed by Harry J. Wild. Both effervescent and timeless, this witty gem showcases Monroe’s brilliant comic timing as well as her vocal chops. Premiering in the middle of the actress’s career and released the same year as Niagara and How to Marry a Millionaire , Howard Hawks’s film helped to plant Monroe in the hearts of the American public, making her one of the most famous people in the US.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Howard Hawks PRODUCED BY: Sol C. Siegel

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Released the same year the first theories of neo-realism were published in film magazines Esprit, La Revue du Cinéma , and Bianco e Nero by acclaimed critics, including André Bazin, Germany Year Zero rounds out Rossellini’s WWII trilogy and brings a continental scope to the devastating impact of Hitler’s final solution. By centering the story on a young boy navigating the devastating implications of war, Rossellini accentuates the stark contrast between generations. A major influence on François Truffaut’s The 400 Blows (1959) and cast with people the director found by exploring the four zones of Berlin, Germany Year Zero would, Rossellini hoped, “reproduce the truth exactly as the camera saw it for that audience through the entire world which has a heart capable of love and a brain capable of thought.”

This lavish, widescreen musical from director Vincente Minnelli received nine Oscar nominations and won in each of its categories, including Best Picture and Directing. Minnelli’s An American in Paris (1951) discovery Leslie Caron plays Gigi, a young woman in turn-of-the-20th-century Paris who catches the eye of a charming womanizer (Louis Jourdan). The Oscar-winning screenplay by Alan Jay Lerner was based on the 1944 novella by Colette, and Lerner wrote the film’s original songs with his My Fair Lady (1964) composer Frederick Loewe, their score including such classics as “I Remember It Well,” “The Night They Invented Champagne,” and the Oscar-winning title song. Art directors William A. Horning and Preston Ames and set decorators Henry Grace and Keogh Gleason won Oscars for their eye-poppingly colorful recreation of the City of Light.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Vincente Minnelli

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: A weekend party at an English mansion in the 1930s leads to murder in this seriocomic whodunit, with Robert Altman directing an all-star cast. The Oscar-winning screenplay came via Julian Fellowes, who later explored the same milieu for Downton Abbey . The remarkable transatlantic cast includes Alan Bates, Bob Balaban (who also produced and came up with the story idea with Altman), Clive Owen, Kristin Scott Thomas, Emily Watson, and Helen Mirren and Maggie Smith, who were both nominated for their performances. The film’s seven nominations include Best Picture, Directing, and Art Direction, with production designer Stephen Altman and set decorator Anna Pinnock mixing authentic English mansions and soundstage sets to evoke the glamour and class divisions of the era.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Robert Altman

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Winner of the Special Jury Prize at the 2023 Venice Film Festival, Holland’s “angry and urgent masterpiece” ( The Guardian ) centers around the 2021 migrant crisis that unfolded in the exclusion zone between Poland and Belarus. Named for the swamplands that cover the region, Holland’s impactful narrative was conceived by reflecting on actual events, using interviews with real border guards and refugees to inform the four interwoven stories that supply the work with its incredible emotional depth. Made with trusted collaborators, including cinematographer Tomasz Naumiuk and co-writer Gabriela Łazarkiewicz-Sieczko, Green Border insists on depicting regional upheaval and conflict by prioritizing its human impact.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Agnieszka Holland PRODUCED BY: Fred Bernstein, Agnieszka Holland, Marcin Wierzchoslawski

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Accessible screening On the last Saturday of every month, the museum's Family Matinee is an accessible screening where we offer open captioning, keep the theater dimly lit, and maintain a lower volume for viewers who are neurodiverse. When Billy receives a mysterious creature called a mogwai, affectionately named Gizmo, from his father for Christmas, he must follow three rules: keep it away from sunlight, don’t get it wet, and above all else, never feed it after midnight. When the creature accidentally gets wet and more mogwai spawn with much more devious intentions than the docile Gizmo, mayhem erupts. With the town’s adults out of their depth, it is up to Billy and Gizmo to defeat these menacing creatures. The violence in the PG-rated Gremlins was one of the reasons the Motion Picture Association later created the PG-13 rating; the film is often cited as kick-starting a trend of small creature features in the 1980s. Please note: This film contains discussions about Santa Claus that might not be appropriate for younger viewers.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Joe Dante PRODUCED BY: Michael Finnell

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: John Sturges ( The Magnificent Seven, 1960 ) directed this vivid re-telling of the classic Western set in 1880s Arizona. Burt Lancaster is Marshal Wyatt Earp, who partners with his brothers to clean up the town of Tombstone. Helped by loyal friend Doc Holliday (Kirk Douglas), they find themselves embroiled in a deadly conflict with the Clanton family. The second film to team Lancaster and Douglas, Gunfight was nominated for its film editing and sound recording and features a rousing score by four-time Oscar winner Dimitri Tiomkin ( High Noon , 1952), with a memorable title song performed by Frankie Laine. In 1967, Sturges continued the story with Hour of the Gun , starring James Garner as Earp and Jason Robards as Holliday.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Sturges

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: On Halloween night, 1963, in the small Illinois town of Haddonfield, 6-year-old Michael Myers commits a horribly violent act against his older sister. Fifteen years later, he escapes from a mental institution, returns to Haddonfield on Halloween, and stalks teenage babysitter Laurie Strode (Jamie Lee Curtis, in her feature film debut) while psychiatrist Dr. Loomis (Donald Pleasence) tries to find him. Released in 1978, Halloween is a pioneering slasher film that established Curtis as a scream queen. Driven by John Carpenter’s sharp direction and staging, coupled with the use of POV shots and his now-iconic, eerie piano score, Halloween went on to become one of the most profitable independent films of all time, leading to numerous sequels, reboots, remakes and many other adaptations.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Carpenter PRODUCED BY: Debra Hill

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: he second installment of the epic Yi Sun-sin trilogy by director Kim Han-min stars Park Hae-il as the 48-year-old Yi Sun-sin, an admiral of the Joseon dynasty (1392-1910) venerated for seemingly miraculous victories over the Japanese naval forces during the Imjin War period. The film focuses on the 1592 Hansan Island battle against a fleet overseen by daimyo (feudal lord) Wakisaka Yasuharu, who plans to conquer the Joseon peninsula on a quest to devour the entire Ming Dynasty. Yi’s famously optimized Turtle battleship appears in grandiose, precisely executed glory under Yi’s orchestration. Spectacular visual compositions, complemented by remarkable visual effects and a magnificent score, come together to deliver one of most gratifying naval war scenes ever shown on the Korean big screen.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Kim Han-min

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: The first motion picture produced by Nickelodeon is also Bronwen Hughes’s feature film directorial debut, starring Michelle Trachtenberg as a 12-year-old Harriet Welsch, who devotes her time spying on everyone and recording her discreet detective work in a “PRIVATE” notebook. When those secrets get exposed, Harriet finds her entire class against her, including her two best friends. This sweet drama boldly and candidly surveys the bittersweet pre-teen years as an exploration of self, complementing the confusion that marks this transitional phase with Harriet’s unapologetic, cheeky spirit, letting her fight her own battles and attain redemption.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Bronwen Hughes

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: On All Hallows’ Eve, skeptical teen Max and little sister Dani are trick-or-treating in their new town of Salem, Massachusetts, when they accidentally resurrect the Sanderson Sisters, three 17th-century witches who were executed after terrorizing the town. The kids must team with Max’s crush, Allison, and Binx, a boy cursed by the sisters to live out eternity as a cat, to put an end to the witches’ reign of terror before the sisters can steal their souls. A box office and critical failure upon release, Hocus Pocus gained cult status through annual Halloween reruns on Disney Channel and the iconic performances from Bette Midler, Sarah Jessica Parker, and Kathy Najimy as the witches.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Kenny Ortega PRODUCED BY: David Kirschner, Steven Haft

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: The stars (Peter Cushing, Christopher Lee), screenwriter (Jimmy Sangster), and director (Terence Fisher) of Hammer Films’ 1957 breakout hit The Curse of Frankenstein reunited for this exciting adaptation of Bram Stoker’s classic novel. Cushing brought subtlety and intelligence to the character of Dr. Van Helsing, which he would play four more times for Hammer, and Lee’s quietly charismatic portrayal of the Count (a role he would reprise in six sequels) made him one of the most iconic interpreters of the role. With its bold Technicolor cinematography by Jack Asher and the thunderous orchestral score by Hammer regular James Bernard, the film helped establish the studio as a brand name in big-screen horror.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Terence Fisher PRODUCED BY: Anthony Hinds

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Based on the unproduced play Next of Kin , Hot Spell is a New Orleans-set drama about matriarch Alma, whose boundless optimism stands at odds with her husband John’s philandering and her adult children’s desire to move on from the family home. Set during one sweltering summer evening, screenwriter James Poe, who also adapted Tennessee Williams’s Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1958), slowly ratchets up the pressure on the tenuous facade of the happy mid-century nuclear family. Starring a trifecta of Oscar winners—Shirley Booth ( Come Back, Little Sheba , 1952), Anthony Quinn ( Wild is the Wind , 1958; Zorba the Greek , 1964), Shirley MacLaine ( Terms of Endearment , 1983)—and supported by another—Eileen Heckart ( Butterflies Are Free , 1972) as Alma’s jaded best friend—this tender, layered production offers a heartbreaking view of generational tensions and the nuances of family dynamics.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Daniel Mann

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: A hapless young backpacker (voiced by Andy Samberg) stumbles upon an Eastern European resort and falls for the owner’s daughter (Selena Gomez), unaware that he’s discovered a hotel for monsters and that his prospective father-in-law is Dracula himself. Adam Sandler leads the stellar comedic voice cast as the Count, with Kevin James as Frankenstein’s monster, Fran Drescher as his bride, Steve Buscemi as a werewolf, and David Spade as the Invisible Man. Director Genndy Tartakovsky’s inventive visuals are an ideal match for the script’s winning mixture of humor and sentiment. The film would spawn three sequels and a TV series.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Genndy Tartakovsky PRODUCED BY: Michelle Murdocca

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Schatze, Pola, and Loco (Lauren Bacall, Marilyn Monroe, Betty Grable) are Manhattan models on a mission to marry rich husbands. Although they set their sights on Vanderbilts and Rockefellers, their plans go awry when they become attracted to men who look to be penniless. How to Marry a Millionaire was released at the end of Monroe’s breakout year, having starred in Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and Niagara in 1953. The film is notable as the first to be completed in CinemaScope, and Monroe had such broad appeal that 20th Century-Fox used her to advertise this new widescreen format: a slogan above an image of Marilyn claimed she was “Big as life and a million times more fun in Cinemascope!”
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Jean Negulesco PRODUCED BY: Nunnally Johnson

When young hatmaker Sophie is transformed into a 90-year-old woman by the vengeful Witch of the Waste, she seeks to break the curse with the help of the enigmatic wizard Howl, the fire demon Calcifer, and the magical moving castle they inhabit.

Ricky Baker (Julian Dennison), a Māori foster teen with a knack for getting into trouble, is placed into the warm care of Bella Faulkner (Rima Te Wiata) and her stern, indifferent husband, Hec (Sam Neill). When an unexpected tragedy strikes, Ricky runs away into the New Zealand bush, obligating Hec to seek him out. Thanks to a set of comical mishaps and misconceptions, the two become subjects of a manhunt, forcing them to go on the run and brave the wilderness. Sam Neill’s portrayal of Hec is one of the actor’s most cherished performances as he deftly evolves from reluctant guardian to a quietly tender father figure for Dennison’s rambunctiously endearing Ricky. Adapted from the 1986 novel Wild Pork and Watercress by Barry Crump, Hunt for the Wilderpeople premiered at the Sundance Film Festival to critical acclaim. The film also broke box office records in New Zealand that year, becoming the most successful film made locally—excluding international co-productions—an achievement the film still holds today.

Jane Campion’s gritty erotic thriller stars Meg Ryan as Frannie Avery, a seemingly apathetic writer and English teacher who finds solace in her daydream of language and literature. At a bar near her apartment, Frannie accidentally witnesses a sexual encounter between a woman and a man whose face she cannot recall. The woman is later found dismembered, spurring a visit from a detective who quickly becomes Frannie’s infatuation. Paralleling the desolate ambience of the urban landscape is Frannie’s facade, until her suppressed emotions trigger outbursts that may lead her straight into the path of a serial killer of women.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Jane Campion

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Directed and scored by John Carpenter, and written by Michael De Luca, this love letter to the work of H. P. Lovecraft sees insurance investigator John Trent (Sam Neill) journey to a mysterious small town, unaware that he is entering the depths of insanity. Taking its name from Lovecraft’s 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness , the final film in the Apocalypse Trilogy follows Trent as he tracks down horror novelist Sutter Cane (Jürgen Prochnow), who has gone missing after completing his latest book. Word spreads that anyone who reads an advance copy of the novel becomes a homicidal maniac, but Trent is convinced it is all a publicity stunt—until his investigation leads him to an eerie town identical to Cane’s work.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Carpenter PRODUCED BY: Sandy King

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Natalie Portman was nominated for her uncanny performance as Jacqueline Bouvier Kennedy in this unusual biopic directed by Pablo Larraín ( Maria , 2024). The screenplay by Noah Oppenheim is structured around an interview by a magazine journalist (Billy Crudup) and focuses on key events in the First Lady’s life, especially the assassination of her husband. The film was also nominated for Madeline Fontaine’s authentic costume designs and the unsettling score by Mica Levi ( Under the Skin , 2013), which used flutes and strings to evoke its heroine’s combination of vulnerability and resilience.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Pablo Larraín

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Park Hae-il plays Lee Won-sang, the hero of Park Chan-ok’s debut feature, in his second big-screen appearance. Lee is a 27-year-old graduate student in literature, finishing up his thesis before he leaves for London. When he starts writing an article for a magazine as a favor, he realizes that the head editor, Han Yun-shik, is the reason his girlfriend left him. Lee’s complicated feelings toward Han, a mixture of admiration and jealousy, brings more confusion when he is introduced to a mesmerizing photographer, Park Sung-yeon, a cool, down-to-earth woman who is also having an affair with Han. Calm on the surface but roiling underneath, the story explores human emotions in a macro lens, excavating endless variables that shape characters while they struggle to stay composed. Park’s undefinable approach to Lee allows his character’s purity and honesty to roam free.

In this filmed version of Paul Claudel and Arthur Honegger’s oratorio, or sung mystery play, Rossellini’s wife, Ingrid Bergman, plays Saint Joan of Arc in the final minutes of her life. Shot in rich Gevacolor, a Belgian affiliate of German Agfacolor, this surreal musical is the fourth of five projects the couple made together. In a 1954 interview, Rossellini said of the project: “It’s a very strange film. I know it will be said that my involution has reached its maximum limit, that I am digging my own grave. It is not a filmed play, it is pure cinema, and I would even go as far as saying it is neorealism as I have always intended it.” A commercial failure on its release, this 35mm screening of an imported 35mm print from Italy is one of the rarest titles featured in this series.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Roberto Rossellini PRODUCED BY: Giorgio Criscuolo, Franco Francese

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: US restoration premiere “It was very important for me to show Italy, Naples,” Rossellini said in 1954, “that strange atmosphere so imbued with a very real, very immediate, very deep feeling: the sense of eternal life.” The fantastic Ingrid Bergman and George Sanders play Katherine and Alex Joyce, an unhappily married English couple of eight years whose trip to Italy takes them along separate, and possibly permanently diverging, paths. Bergman’s fourth film with then-husband Roberto Rossellini allows her to relax into a natural acting style that would become a blueprint for 1960s actors and filmmakers interested in presenting fresh, grounded performances.

Following their collaborations on Taxi Driver (1976), Raging Bull (1980), and others, two-time Oscar-winning actor Robert De Niro and Oscar-winning director Martin Scorsese re-teamed for this dark comedy. Zealous aspiring comic Rupert Pupkin collaborates with an obsessive fangirl (Sandra Bernhard) to kidnap their favorite late-night host (Jerry Lewis). A critical darling that was a box office failure upon its release, the film has since become a pop-culture touchstone, thanks to social media and its empty promises of celebrity access. Actor Jason Bateman has called this one of his favorite films; he joins Turner Classic Movies host Dave Karger for a conversation about it after the screening. In a separately ticketed event before the screening, Karger signs copies of his new book , 50 Movie Nights: Contemporary Stars on Their Favorite Films , at the Academy Museum Store.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Martin Scorsese PRODUCED BY: Arnon Milchan

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Just after Agnieszka Holland completed film school in Prague, Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda, already an established and celebrated auteur for films like Ashes and Diamonds (1958), welcomed the young aspirant to visit his set of The Wedding (1973). Over time, Holland said, “our relation moved from ‘master–pupil’ to something much more equal in collaboration and friendship,” and she started to write scripts with him. One of their most meaningful collaborations was this 1990 biopic about the extraordinary Polish-Jewish humanitarian Janusz Korczak, remembered “for his pedagogical philosophy and his heroic actions during the Holocaust,” Holland told the BFI. With stunning cinematography by Robby Müller ( Dead Man , 1995), Korczak is, as Steven Spielberg once wrote, "one of the most important European pictures about the Holocaust."
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Andrzej Wajda PRODUCED BY: Janusz Morgenstern, Willi Segler, Daniel Toscan du Plantier, Regina Ziegler

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: “I’ve made films in episodes because I feel more at ease like that.” —Roberto Rossellini, 1952 Rossellini’s appreciation for episodic storytelling, which his later forays into television allowed him to explore with more freedom, first began in feature-length filmmaking. Part one, titled “Una voce umana,” is based on a play by Jean Cocteau and features the filmmaker’s then-lover, esteemed actress Anna Magnani, known only as the woman on the phone, speaking to a former flame. In part two, “Il miracolo,” a woman is sure she is pregnant with the child of a saint. Dubbed the best foreign film that year by New York critics, Amore was also met with derision when Rossellini was charged with blasphemy by the city’s archbishop due to the content of the film’s second half.

Bong Joon Ho’s phenomenal breakthrough film stars Park Hae-il as an enigmatic young loner and observer whose innocent demeanor seems too wholesome to be true. Inspired by a true story, Memories of Murder centers around the gruesome serial killings of women in South Korea in the 1980s, investigated by Doo-man (Song Kang-ho), a detective who relies on instinct rather than fact. Bong’s vision, which challenges conventional components of storytelling and blurs the boundaries between genres, is meticulously orchestrated in this crime thriller, and Park’s elegantly simple depiction of a complicated character is phenomenal.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Bong Joon Ho

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: A New York police officer is recruited into a secret government organization that helps hide the existence of extraterrestrial visitors from the public, and teams up with a more experienced operative to track down a malicious alien that has taken over a human host. Tommy Lee Jones and Will Smith make an unexpectedly ideal mismatched pair of heroes, later reuniting for two sequels, and are supported by witty performances from Linda Fiorentino, Rip Torn, and a physical tour-de-force from Vincent D’Onofrio as the possessed farmer. Rick Baker and David LeRoy Anderson won Oscars for their imaginative alien makeup designs; Danny Elfman was nominated for his lively score; and production designer Bo Welch and set decorator Cheryl Carasik were nominated for the film’s art direction, which deftly combined retro-futurist sets and authentic New York locations.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Barry Sonnenfeld

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Dr. Barnaby Fulton (Cary Grant) is a scatterbrained chemist working to create an elixir of youth. When one of his chimpanzees, Esther, breaks loose, she mixes chemicals in Barnaby’s lab, dumping the concoction into the office’s water cooler. The formula generates the rejuvenation effect Barnaby has been seeking — along with more chaotic side effects in some cases. Monkey Business allowed Monroe, who co-stars as Lois Laurel, to showcase her brilliant timing, further solidifying her reputation as a comedic actress.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Howard Hawks PRODUCED BY: Sol C. Siegel

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Hae-guk (Park Hae-il) receives word that his estranged father has passed away, bringing him to an unusual village for the funeral. Sensing his presence is unwelcome, Hae-guk grows suspicious and begins to sense a deeper truth behind his father's death . Adapted from a Korean webtoon, Moss submerges audiences in a dark and thrilling mystery, blending suspense and horror to create a world of uncertainty. –Note written by Hannah Farkas.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Kang Woo-suk

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: After the killing of Israeli hostages at the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, a Mossad agent (Eric Bana) assembles a team to assassinate the men deemed responsible for the murders. Steven Spielberg’s fact-based international thriller is a thoughtful look at the moral costs of violence, with gripping suspense and an impressive supporting cast including Best Actor winner Geoffrey Rush ( Shine , 1996), Supporting Actor nominee Ciarán Hinds ( Belfast , 2021), and Daniel Craig, shortly before he debuted as James Bond. The film received five Oscar nominations including Best Picture, Directing, and , for John Williams’ music, his 22nd feature score for the director. Williams’s somber, restrained score focused on, in the composer’s words, “the enormous suffering and guilt, and eventually, paranoia” of Bana’s protagonist.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Steven Spielberg

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: My Dad Is 100 Years Old This short tribute casts celebrated actress Isabella Rossellini as herself as well as various filmmakers who influenced or were influenced by her father, filmmaker Roberto Rossellini. Conceived by Isabella on the eve of her father’s centenary, she took a “docu-fantasia” concept to avant-garde filmmaker Guy Maddin after her delightful experience on his 2003 feature, The Saddest Music in the World. A beautiful cinema poem for a beloved father and artist.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Guy Maddin PRODUCED BY: Jody Shapiro

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Emma Roberts steps into the role of Nancy Drew in this contemporary adaptation of the iconic teen detective. When Nancy’s father (Tate Donovan) gets a job that moves them to Los Angeles, he encourages her to behave like an average teenager and refrain from sleuthing. Unable to refrain from her passion, Nancy dives into a famous cold case involving the death of a movie star. The subject of hundreds of novels, and numerous film, television and video game adaptations, the character of Nancy Drew has been inspiring young women since the 1930s.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Andrew Fleming

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Newlyweds Ray and Polly Cutler (Jean Peters and Casey Adams) take a postponed honeymoon at Niagara Falls, where they encounter Rose and George Loomis (Marilyn Monroe and Joseph Cotten). The Loomis’s rocky relationship hangs over the couple’s romantic getaway, further complicated by a murder. 1953 was an important year for Monroe with the successes of Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and How to Marry a Millionaire in the following months, and her breakout performance as the sensual Rose in Niagara catapulted the actor into superstardom.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Henry Hathaway PRODUCED BY: Charles Brackett

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Hitchcock plays with the concept of the wrong man, a frequent theme in his narratives, in one of the most admired and entertaining of his mid-career films. North by Northwest stars four-time collaborator Grant as Roger O. Thornhill, a suave ad executive whose identity is mistaken for a government agent. Ruthless spy Philip Vandamm (James Mason) is after Thornhill; on a separate mission is a group of secret agents who follows Thornhill across the country. On the run, Thornhill meets Eve Kendall, a mesmerizing, peculiar woman whose mysterious identity amplifies the level of danger he is in. The film’s ironically ecstatic tone parallels the enchanting aspect of Grant’s portrayal of Thornhill—elegantly sarcastic with a witty sense of humor. Processed in Technicolor, this spectacular thriller showcases now-iconic action sequences such as the crop duster plane chase and climax at Mount Rushmore.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Alfred Hitchcock

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Quentin Tarantino’s alternate history of the late-’60s film scene focuses on the intertwining lives of three figures: fading TV Western star Rick Dalton (Best Actor nominee Leonardo DiCaprio), his stunt double and best friend Cliff Booth (Supporting Actor winner Brad Pitt) and the real-life starlet Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie), whose life is destined to cross paths with Charles Manson and his followers. With its massive, stellar cast (including Margaret Qualley, Timothy Olyphant, Austin Butler, Dakota Fanning, Bruce Dern, Damian Lewis, and Al Pacino) and evocative, needle-drop score, Once Upon a Time elegantly evokes a lost era of Hollywood. Nominated for 10 Oscars including Best Picture, it won for production designer Barbara Ling and set decorator Nancy Haigh, who incorporate real-life locations such as the Musso & Frank Grill and the Playboy Mansion while creating believable living spaces for the protagonists.

Paul Thomas Anderson won Oscars for Directing, Adapted Screenplay and Best Picture (along with fellow producers Adam Somner and Sara Murphy) for his epic comedy-thriller, loosely based on Thomas Pynchon’s 1990 novel Vineland , about a retired revolutionary (Best Actor nominee Leonardo DiCaprio) trying to protect his teenage daughter from a fanatical military officer (Supporting Actor winner Sean Penn). Anderson’s longtime casting director Cassandra Kulukundis won the Academy’s inaugural Oscar for Casting, her expertly chosen ensemble including past Oscar winners (including Supporting Actor nominee Benicio Del Toro), veteran character actors, comedy writers, and impressive newcomers such as Chase Infiniti, who plays DiCaprio’s daughter.

Marlon Brando took on his only feature directing project—following the last-minute departure of original director Stanley Kubrick—with this character-oriented Western about a bank robber who tracks down a friend (frequent Brando co-star Karl Malden) who betrayed him. The Academy Award–nominated VistaVision color cinematography by Charles Lang Jr. ( How the West Was Won ,1962) makes strong use of scenic locations in Mexico and California, with vivid imagery of Brando riding his horse along the Monterey coastline. Until 2024, One-Eyed Jacks was the final film shot with the VistaVision process.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Marlon Brando

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: The memoir of Danish author Karen Blixen (published under her pen name Isak Dinesen) was adapted by director Sydney Pollack and screenwriter Kurt Leudtke for this lavish romantic drama, focusing on the years Blixen (Best Actress nominee Meryl Streep) spent running a coffee farm in Nairobi and her relationship with hunter Denys Finch-Hatton (Robert Redford). Out of Africa was nominated for 11 Oscars and won seven including Best Picture, Directing (both for Pollack), Adapted Screenplay, Art Direction, Cinematography and Sound, with John Barry winning his fourth Oscar for an achingly romantic score.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Sydney Pollack

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Bank robber Jake Foley’s prison escape is complicated by an inconvenient encounter with U.S. marshal Karen Sisco, and an unexpected attraction between them. Making his first major studio film, director Steven Soderbergh, working with an Oscar nominated screenplay by Scott Frank, brings the world of master crime novelist Elmore Leonard to the screen in a dazzling combination of old-fashioned Hollywood glamour and contemporary grit. The film was also nominated for its editing, by the accomplished Anne V. Coates ( Lawrence of Arabia, 1962), who employs intercutting, flashbacks, and freeze frames to enhance the swooningly romantic chemistry of stars George Clooney and Jennifer Lopez.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Steven Soderbergh

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: The second installment in his WWII trilogy and one of Rossellini’s favorites of his films, the episodic Paisàn is another depiction of the tribulations of the Italians under German occupation. Its title translates to “fellow countryman” and takes a broader view of Italy than his previous Rome, Open City (1945) , moving the action outside the capital to focus on the interactions between American armed forces and the country residents impacted by conflict. Future Italian auteur Federico Fellini co-wrote the screenplay, which came together on the fly, with dialogue of each sequence written just before it was filmed.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Roberto Rossellini PRODUCED BY: Rod E. Geiger, Roberto Rossellini

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Ofelia (Ivana Baquero), a 10-year-old girl in Francoist Spain, discovers a magical underworld in one of writer-director Guillermo del Toro’s most richly imagined fantasies. When Ofelia is lured into a labyrinth hidden in the forest, a faun emerges to reveal she is a long-lost princess. To return to her mystical kingdom, Ofelia must complete three magical tasks. The film earned six Academy Award nominations , including Foreign Language Film, and won for its stunning Art Direction, Cinematography, and Makeup, with del Toro regular Doug Jones playing the Faun and the Pale Man. Pan’s Labyrinth appears here in a brand-new 4K restoration and in 3D. Del Toro, who personally supervised every stage of the new restoration from the original 35mm negative, introduces the film in person. Special thanks to Cineverse.

Ponyo focuses on the friendship between 5-year-old Sosuke and a magical goldfish named Brunhilde, the young daughter of a sorcerer father and a sea-goddess mother. After wandering away from her father’s four-flippered submarine, Brunhilde washes ashore and is discovered by the curious Sosuke. Now renamed Ponyo, she forms a quick bond with Sosuke that fuels her yearning to be a real girl, and together they shoulder the cost of what that might take. The vibrant and colorful hand-drawn animations are a delight for audiences of all ages, as Hayao Miyazaki builds a world filled with magical goldfish, spellcasters, and sea goddesses in this tale of how friendships can blossom anywhere—even in the ocean’s depths.

The first film directed by a woman to receive the Queer Palm at the Cannes Film Festival, Céline Sciamma’s 18th-century romance revels in the sensuous affair between aristocrat Héloïse (Adèle Haenel) and artist Marianne (Noémie Merlant), who is commissioned to paint her portrait. Though betrothed to a wealthy man of the Milanese upper class, the stubborn Héloïse refuses to be captured, either by her male suitor or the artist meant to paint her. Sciamma’s tale of sexual liberation finds beauty in the electric connection between her leading women for a gorgeous and aching story of forbidden love and the fleeting nature of romance.

Quantum physics Professor Howard Birack (Victor Wong) tasks his students with their most unusual assignment yet when a Catholic priest (Donald Pleasence) uncovers a strange and ancient substance in a monastery. As the young scientists investigate, dark entities descend upon the church, bringing representatives of Satan to the Earthly plane. John Carpenter wrote, directed, and co-scored Prince of Darkness as the second chapter in his Apocalypse Trilogy, which begins with The Thing (1982), and finishes with In the Mouth of Madness (1995).
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: John Carpenter PRODUCED BY: Larry J. Franco

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: An ordinary woman survives a near-death experience and discovers newfound powers of healing in this supernaturally tinged drama, directed by Daniel Petrie ( A Raisin in the Sun , 1961) from an original screenplay by Lewis John Carlino ( The Great Santini , 1979) that emphasizes character and emotion over fantasy. Resurrection was a passion project for actress Ellen Burstyn, who worked closely with Carlino to develop the screenplay, receiving a Best Actress nomination for her subtle, heartfelt work. Theater legend Eva Le Gallienne was also nominated for her thoughtful performance as Burstyn’s grandmother, three-time Oscar winner Maurice Jarre ( Lawrence of Arabia , 1962) composed the soaring score, and the striking visual effects for the afterlife sequence were created by Tony Silver and Oscar nominees Richard Greenberg and Robert Greenberg ( Predator, 1987).
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Daniel Petrie PRODUCED BY: Renée Missel, Howard Rosenman

https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.description: Marilyn Monroe’s appearance in Western genre films required designer Travilla to create costumes ranging from saloon-style gowns to casual denim looks. Monroe wanted her character, Kay—a kind-hearted saloon singer torn between an ex-convict (Robert Mitchum) and her troubled fiancé (Rory Calhoun)—to have a natural feel. Her acting coach, Natasha Lytess, and director Otto Preminger clashed over whether Monroe should use her typical breathy voice, with the studio backing Monroe’s decision to forgo it.
https://www.academymuseum.org/en/program.director: Otto Preminger PRODUCED BY: Stanley Rubin
